items.title: Freeze the evaluation and resource contract
items.claim: Make comparable pilot measurements possible before spending another training budget.
items.basis: Both dev and confirmation have been inspected; many saved predictions exist but are not training out-of-fold predictions. Attempt 002 is the frozen reference.
items.first_test: Inventory exact split IDs, checkpoint/config hashes and cached predictions; specify grouped inner folds within the training partition, a matched baseline, selection rules, paired group bootstrap and a fixed pilot. Refresh Kaggle quota/job status and profile candidate fit before any GPU launch.
items.acceptance: Commit a protocol with artifact paths, baseline metrics on identical rows, a small predeclared search budget, nested grouped selection and per-job runtime caps. Count baseline retraining and OOF generation explicitly when needed. No GPU launch is needed just to write the protocol.
items.stop: Do not start downstream pilots if split/provenance, remaining quota, checkpoint availability or a feasible runtime budget is unresolved.
items.risk_reason: Reusing inspected folds can create optimistic selection; stale quota and hidden-row assumptions can invalidate a runtime plan.
items.mitigation: Label existing folds exploratory; use nested grouped selection and new independent data if available. Verify current quota and test-row count assumptions at launch.
items.rationale: Prevents spending compute on incomparable changes or promoting validation overfit.
items.revision: Added a prerequisite outside the forty hypotheses; this is evaluation work, not a forecast of score gain.

items.title: Preference-trained backbone
items.claim: A preference-trained reward backbone may encode useful human-preference distinctions beyond the chat classifier.
items.basis: Historical preference-model recipes motivate this; our general prompted judge did not establish an advantage. No selected reward checkpoint has been tested locally.
items.first_test: Verify a public Skywork/ArmoRM candidate license, provenance, input template, Kaggle attachment and memory. Score both answers on a training-only mapping set and a fixed pilot; cross-fit a symmetric three-class head rather than treating one reward scalar as class probabilities.
items.acceptance: Advance only if mapped probabilities beat the matched frozen classifier on the pilot and runtime/provenance pass. Adopt after larger paired evaluation under E00.
items.stop: Defer the checkpoint if it cannot fit/run offline, known evaluation overlap is unresolved, or the mapping adds no signal over the baseline.
items.risk_reason: Public reward training can overlap this public benchmark; scalar rewards omit tie probabilities, and an 8B model may exceed runtime.
items.mitigation: Audit known training data and unknown exposure separately; fit the tie/winner mapping only within folds; profile two-answer inference before scaling.
items.rationale: A relatively cheap frozen-model pilot tests a different training objective before another full fine-tune.
items.revision: Reward models are not ready-made three-class classifiers, and checkpoint availability is not proof of clean evaluation.

items.title: Larger supervised classifier
items.claim: An 8–9B supervised preference classifier may learn distinctions missed by Qwen3-4B.
items.basis: Capacity is plausible but the blind assistant comparison was inconclusive; size alone has not been isolated.
items.first_test: Fit/profile one larger candidate, then compare short training curves at matched examples/tokens and packing. Report a separate equal-wall-budget comparison.
items.acceptance: A larger matched-exposure evaluation improves overall loss and has a feasible quantized submission path.
items.stop: Stop if memory/throughput prevents useful exposure, or pilot loss does not improve enough to justify the cost.
items.risk_reason: A larger model can see fewer examples within quota and require multiple nine-hour jobs; teacher/data exposure may differ.
items.mitigation: Separate model size from data, packing and token exposure; use exact resumable checkpoints and record provenance.
items.rationale: Potentially material but more expensive and less directly supported than first-wave changes.
items.revision: Model level and model size are not interchangeable; compare training objective and exposure as well as parameters.

items.title: Broader adapter coverage
items.claim: Adapting feed-forward layers as well as attention may improve preference representations.

items.acceptance: Overall paired loss improves after matching exposure/calibration; memory and inference artifacts remain valid.
items.stop: Stop if added optimizer memory prevents useful batches or gains disappear when adapter parameter count is controlled.
items.risk_reason: Changing both coverage and parameter budget confounds the result; extra optimizer state reduces throughput.
items.mitigation: Measure trainable parameters and tokens/second; use a matched-rank-budget ablation before a full run.
items.rationale: A contained training change with useful precedent and less deployment complexity than a new architecture.
items.revision: Broader coverage is not automatically better; isolate coverage from total adaptation capacity.

items.title: Better optimization
items.claim: Learning-rate, warmup or batch choices may have limited the current classifier.
items.basis: The late learning curve plateau is observed; its cause has not been identified. H03 one-epoch continuation improves full-dev loss0.014803 with positive group evidence; raw fixed selection losses1400/1438 are0.949402/0.949409. The final flat interval under the ending schedule does not diagnose the learning-rate cause or justify an automatic second epoch.
items.first_test: Predeclare at most three schedules on the same training-only pilot; compare matched tokens and one selected full run, counting the whole search cost.
items.acceptance: A selected schedule improves a larger evaluation rather than only the best noisy pilot checkpoint.
items.stop: Stop the grid if training is already stable and no schedule improves the predeclared learning-curve criterion.
items.risk_reason: Searching many schedules or checkpoints overfits dev and silently multiplies GPU cost.
items.mitigation: Cap the grid, use inner folds for selection and report all curves including failed runs.
items.rationale: Useful only with a small disciplined search; do not use an open-ended hyperparameter sweep.
items.revision: The plateau does not specifically diagnose the learning rate. Compare any future schedule against the accepted step1438 reference with matched exposure and postprocessing; completed H03 is not a license to run more epochs.

history.note: Record supported one-epoch continuation and nearly flat final selection interval. Future optimization uses latest matched reference; no automatic second epoch or schedule search executed.

items.title: Response-aware pooling
items.claim: Separate learned pooling over each answer may expose comparison features more directly than the current final-token head.
items.basis: The deployed model pools a final token. That token already has causal access to both answers; no information-access defect is established.
items.first_test: Add masked A/B pooled representations and a small comparison head while retaining the same causal backbone and packing.
items.acceptance: Matched-exposure overall loss improves; answer-swap equivariance and padding/masking invariants pass.
items.stop: Stop if feature pooling adds no discrimination or only reduces training loss.
items.risk_reason: Incorrect token spans/padding can leak position or mix question and answer evidence.
items.mitigation: Test token-span masks, swapped examples and short/long inputs before training.
items.rationale: A controlled architecture ablation, after cheaper training changes.
items.revision: Final-token pooling may be suboptimal, but it does see both answers.

items.title: Bidirectional comparison attention
items.claim: Changing the attention mask might improve within-answer representations for comparison.
items.basis: The final classification token can already attend to the entire retained question and both answers. A causal model is not missing answer B at classification time.
items.first_test: Only after simpler alternatives, verify mask/kernel support and compare a bidirectional fine-tune with the causal model at matched exposure.
items.acceptance: An end-to-end classifier improves overall loss and retains a compatible offline inference implementation.
items.stop: Defer if custom attention breaks optimized kernels or early validation regresses.
items.risk_reason: Changing the pretrained attention regime may damage representations and remove fast kernels.
items.mitigation: Keep the causal baseline; run a small compatibility/quality probe before any full training.
items.rationale: The original motivation overstated a limitation; high engineering risk and weak local evidence.
items.revision: Corrected: causal attention is not a missing-context bug in our final-token classifier.

items.title: Inference quantization sensitivity
items.claim: Inference precision may account for a small part of preference error.
items.basis: The classifier was trained with a four-bit base. No matched-weight precision ablation has been run.
items.first_test: Compare the same effective trained weights at feasible precisions on fixed rows; explicitly distinguish dequantizing an NF4-trained base from replacing it with the original full-precision base.
items.acceptance: A real paired quality gain survives memory/runtime checks and unchanged calibration protocol.
items.stop: Stop if higher precision cannot fit, or the candidate changes base weights and can no longer isolate inference quantization.
items.risk_reason: Merging adapters onto original BF16 weights changes the effective model; BF16 export does not undo QLoRA training quantization.
items.mitigation: Document exact base/adapter/merge operations and hashes; do not describe a different base as the same-weight precision test.
items.rationale: Likely a small effect, with memory cost and a subtle comparability problem.
items.revision: Narrowed to inference sensitivity; it does not estimate the benefit of full-precision training.

items.title: Explicit swap consistency
items.claim: Paired-view consistency regularization may reduce harmful position dependence beyond existing random swapping and inference averaging.
items.basis: 38.1% raw decision flips and an 8.3-point second-position advantage were measured on the pilot; swap averaging is already deployed.
items.first_test: Compare paired CE alone with paired CE plus symmetric KL on aligned A/B probabilities; preserve ties. Include a matched-token and an equal-wall-budget comparison with random augmentation.
items.acceptance: Lower overall loss after the same swap averaging/calibration, with reduced raw order disagreement and no class collapse.
items.stop: Stop if the regularizer only makes predictions equally uncertain or duplicates the benefit already obtained by averaging.
items.risk_reason: Two views increase compute; excessive consistency can suppress useful discrimination.
items.mitigation: Cap the penalty search, monitor per-class entropy and raw versus averaged metrics, and count both forward passes.
items.rationale: Directly targets the strongest measured model defect with a falsifiable change.
items.revision: The baseline already includes swapping and averaging; estimate only their incremental training-time extension.

items.title: Shared response utilities
items.claim: Shared question-answer scoring may enforce useful A/B symmetry, at the cost of some direct pair interaction.
items.basis: Position instability is measured, but it does not prove independent utility scoring is the best remedy.
items.first_test: Score (question,A) and (question,B) with shared weights; use their difference plus symmetric tie features. Compare with the joint cross-encoder under matched exposure.
items.acceptance: Overall loss and raw order stability improve without a disproportionate failure on subtle pairwise comparisons.
items.stop: Stop if loss of direct cross-answer interaction outweighs improved symmetry.
items.risk_reason: An answer can be useful only relative to its competitor; independent scores can miss these interactions and repeat question processing.
items.mitigation: Keep a joint baseline and measure equal-budget throughput; add only a small symmetric comparison head.
items.rationale: Potentially useful, but a larger architectural change than H09/H11.
items.revision: Shared utilities are not guaranteed to dominate a cross-encoder; direct interaction is a real tradeoff.

items.title: Learned symmetric tie model
items.claim: A learned tie representation constrained to be symmetric may improve tie discrimination.
items.basis: Tie recall is 45.4% and tie AUC 0.668; simple tie-intercept calibration already showed only a small uncertain gain.
items.first_test: Learn p(tie) from symmetric pair features and conditional A/B preference from antisymmetric features. Compare with a three-logit head at matched capacity and supervision.
items.acceptance: Overall paired loss and tie discrimination improve, rather than tie recall increasing through an indiscriminate tie bias.
items.stop: Stop if the only change is algebraically rewriting the same logits, or gains vanish against class-specific calibration.
items.risk_reason: Factorizing a distribution alone adds no information; a separate head can inflate tie predictions.
items.mitigation: Require changed learned features/objective, keep a matched-head control, and report tie AUC, precision/recall and class losses.
items.rationale: Targets a measured weakness with limited inference overhead, while acknowledging an existing calibration control.
items.revision: Rewritten: a two-stage probability formula alone cannot improve the model.

items.title: Soft targets for repeated votes
items.claim: Training-only equivalent comparisons can share a vote distribution, with very limited expected global impact.
items.basis: The entire audit found only 39 canonical repeated-comparison groups covering 123 rows; the conflicting training subset is smaller.
items.first_test: Count usable within-training-fold conflicting groups and compute an optimistic coverage bound before considering any retrain.
items.acceptance: Proceed beyond the CPU audit only if coverage and a plausible effect justify the cost; otherwise retain the result as a negative finding.
items.stop: Do not train a model solely for a signal affecting a tiny fraction of rows without stronger evidence.
items.risk_reason: Tiny counts make empirical soft labels unstable, and cross-fold aggregation would leak targets.
items.mitigation: Aggregate only inside each training fold, align swapped labels, smooth counts and never alter evaluation targets.
items.rationale: Low-cost coverage audit, but not a credible explanation for a 0.17 loss gap.
items.revision: Demoted substantially: repeated conflicting comparisons are rare. GPU estimate covers only the CPU-first scope; any later retrain needs a new budget.

items.title: Noise-robust training loss
items.claim: A robust objective may reduce sensitivity to inconsistent training votes, but could also suppress valid minority preferences.
items.basis: Some identical-answer votes are inconsistent; disagreement with objective correctness is not itself label noise. Extreme wrong cases are not most of the loss.
items.first_test: Predeclare one bounded or bootstrapped objective against CE on identical folds and exposure; evaluate original votes.
items.acceptance: Overall multiclass log loss improves, including minority and tie slices, after identical postprocessing.
items.stop: Stop if the objective improves training stability but worsens calibrated CE or drops unusual valid preferences.
items.risk_reason: The official metric rewards human vote probabilities, not an automatically corrected notion of factual truth.
items.mitigation: Never relabel evaluation data or remove examples just because a model disagrees; keep ordinary CE as control.
items.rationale: Worth a controlled test only after higher-evidence changes.
items.revision: Replaced the assumption that difficult or idiosyncratic votes are necessarily incorrect.

items.title: Criterion-level auxiliary supervision
items.claim: Reliable criterion annotations may help learn instruction compliance and factual consistency while retaining human preference as the primary target.
items.basis: Reviewed failures show such mistakes, but selected error cases do not establish their population frequency or causal importance.
items.first_test: Create a train-only representative annotation pilot with criterion definitions, independent checks and a CE-plus-auxiliary ablation.
items.acceptance: Human-vote loss improves overall; criterion accuracy alone is insufficient.
items.stop: Stop if annotations are unreliable or auxiliary gains fail to transfer to preference predictions.
items.risk_reason: Annotation is expensive and may encode the annotator/teacher rubric rather than voter preference.
items.mitigation: Audit annotation reliability; cap auxiliary weights and preserve the original winner target.
items.rationale: A common annotation foundation for H18/H19, but expensive and unproven.
items.revision: Criterion correctness is an auxiliary signal, not an interchangeable replacement for the competition target.

items.title: Preference-teacher distillation
items.claim: A demonstrated stronger preference teacher may provide useful soft labels for a compact student.
items.basis: Historical solutions used distillation; our current general judge has not demonstrated a reliable improvement over LoRA.
items.first_test: First establish teacher advantage and calibration on the same pilot. Distill a training-only small soft-label set into the student before generating full-dataset teacher predictions.
items.acceptance: The student improves human-vote loss and submission throughput. Report teacher, student and ordinary-supervision controls.
items.stop: Stop if the teacher is no better, only transfers its own bias, or full label generation has no feasible approved compute path.
items.risk_reason: Teacher contamination, uncertain teacher advantage and labeling cost can dominate the experiment.
items.mitigation: Use held-out-group teacher evaluation and provenance checks. Budget assumes a teacher up to roughly 9B fitting two T4s; larger teachers need a separate resource estimate and authorization for any external text service.
items.rationale: One of the larger upside hypotheses, gated on a real teacher advantage instead of model reputation.
items.revision: Do not use the present Gemma or assistant as a proven teacher. The existing Eliza embedding authorization is not blanket authorization for other external APIs.

history.note: No demonstrated teacher advantage from the current candidates: the H01 reward pilot is worse than LoRA, and the prior general judge official score is also worse. Revisit after a stronger teacher is measured, before full distillation cost.
Audit one public winning teacher training repository at exact commit05ac9b9; check whether its final merged folds include our development and confirmation targets before considering distillation.

Exact-commit audit shows final public teacher merges five adapters trained on original competition votes; independent local teacher advantage cannot be established on our cohorts. No weights/soft-label generation or distillation. Require provenance excluding eval groups.

items.title: Refusal appropriateness
items.claim: Request-conditioned refusal features may improve applicable cases beyond a generic refusal penalty.
items.basis: One-sided refusal occurs in 6,075 rows; the non-refusing answer wins about 53%, far from a deterministic rule.
items.first_test: Audit a train-only stratified sample for warranted/unwarranted refusal, then test a request-conditioned auxiliary feature/head.
items.acceptance: Improve refusal-slice and overall loss without penalizing appropriate restraint.
items.stop: Stop if the detector adds no signal beyond current text embeddings or only raises non-refusal bias.
items.risk_reason: A refusal regex is an imperfect English descriptor; treating every refusal as bad gives wrong preferences.
items.mitigation: Manually audit the detector and distinguish the request context; keep this a conditional feature.
items.rationale: There is measurable coverage but weak evidence for a large global gain.
items.revision: Refusal association is not a deterministic target rule or evidence of leakage.

items.title: Additional public preference data
items.claim: Clean, compatible additional comparisons may improve coverage beyond the 46K training partition.
items.basis: The historical recipe used external data; our current data coverage is limited, but compatible uncontaminated additions have not been established.
items.first_test: Audit one candidate dataset license/source/target semantics, remove known exact and semantic overlaps, then compare a small mixed-data pilot with original-only training.
items.acceptance: Improve loss on original human-vote data with stable class/domain behavior; document every added source and mixing ratio.
items.stop: Exclude sources with unresolved provenance/overlap or mismatched preference semantics; stop if mixing hurts the original distribution.
items.risk_reason: Public preference sets may reproduce evaluation examples or teach a different label convention.
items.mitigation: Deduplicate against all known partitions without using their labels; record remaining unknown exposure and avoid claiming fully clean pretraining.
items.rationale: Potentially broader improvement than handcrafted rules, with substantial data-validity risk.
items.revision: Extra data is not automatically clean or useful; provenance and overlap audit precede training.

history.note: Begin CPU-only source/target/overlap audit. Check original LMSYS33K access without accepting account-sharing terms; audit one pinned open UltraFeedback split if gated. No mixed-data GPUtraining funded.

items.title: Controlled instruction counterexamples
items.claim: Verified minimal instruction violations may teach useful distinctions absent from sparse winner labels.
items.basis: The poster contains missed constraints, but their full-dataset frequency is not measured.
items.first_test: Build train-only matched pairs for checkable constraints and compare a small synthetic mixing ratio with original data only.
items.acceptance: Improve human-vote loss on both representative rows and constraint slices without a format-only shortcut.
items.stop: Stop if gains occur only on the synthetic generation template.
items.risk_reason: Synthetic preference labels can impose ideal compliance when real voters prefer other qualities.
items.mitigation: Verify constraints automatically, diversify templates and retain original preference supervision as the main objective.
items.rationale: Cheaper to verify than arbitrary factual claims, after establishing an annotation contract. Annotation tooling can be shared with H14 without waiting for that full experiment.
items.revision: Synthetic constraint truth does not prove the preferred class for an original ambiguous comparison.

items.title: Verified factual counterexamples
items.claim: Independently verified factual mutations may improve discrimination between fluent truth and invention.
items.basis: Factual errors appear in reviewed cases, but a stronger blind judge still makes many preference errors.
items.first_test: Create a small train-only set of matched factual mutations, independently verify both versions, and test a low mixing ratio.
items.acceptance: Human-vote loss improves beyond the mutation templates, with no tie/creative-task regression.
items.stop: Stop if fact checking is unreliable, text artifacts reveal the synthetic winner, or only factual auxiliary accuracy improves.
items.risk_reason: Synthetic artifacts and factuality/preference mismatch can create a misleading benchmark.
items.mitigation: Blind verification, balanced surface edits and separate factuality versus preference metrics.
items.rationale: Potential knowledge benefit, but high annotation cost and uncertain target transfer. Annotation tooling can be shared with H14 without waiting for that full experiment.
items.revision: Factual correctness alone is not the human preference label.

items.title: Out-of-fold hard-example sampling
items.claim: Training examples persistently difficult out of fold may deserve modest additional exposure.
items.basis: Current high-loss poster cases include ambiguous or inconsistent votes, so training residuals are not automatically learnable mistakes.
items.first_test: Generate genuinely OOF training predictions, inspect coverage, then compare capped sampling weights with uniform training.
items.acceptance: Improve overall loss without worsening calibration or minority/tie preferences.
items.stop: Stop if high-loss rows are mostly unstable labels or the gain disappears after OOF selection.
items.risk_reason: Mining in-sample or evaluation errors leaks selection information; hard sampling can amplify noise.
items.mitigation: Generate predictions from models excluding each training group; cap weights and report the original-distribution metric.
items.rationale: Requires expensive OOF generation and has a weak causal basis so far.
items.revision: Existing sampled training predictions are in-sample, not eligible OOF mining scores.

items.title: Domain-aware sampling
items.claim: A carefully limited sampling change may help underlearned domains if reliable domain gaps are found.
items.basis: Code/math/language slices have uncertain labels and different difficulty; underrepresentation has not been established as the cause.
items.first_test: Audit train-only domain labels and counts, then compare capped reweighting with the natural mixture at identical exposure.
items.acceptance: Improve original-distribution overall loss as well as the targeted slices.
items.stop: Stop if only a balanced-domain macro metric improves while the competition mixture worsens.
items.risk_reason: Equalizing domains changes the learning distribution away from the evaluation distribution.
items.mitigation: Use mild capped weights, retain natural-mixture validation and audit detector errors.
items.rationale: Conditional on evidence of underlearning; balancing is not a default fix.
items.revision: Replaced the unsupported assertion that frequent domains crowd out the others.

items.title: Repeated-prompt reweighting
items.claim: Capping each repeated training prompt contribution might improve generalization to new prompt groups.
items.basis: There are 3,286 repeated-prompt groups covering 9,550 rows; this is broader than repeated exact comparisons.
items.first_test: Calculate training-group exposure weights and compare capped weights with natural-frequency training on the same grouped split.
items.acceptance: Overall natural-mixture loss improves, not only unweighted group-average loss.
items.stop: Stop if repeated prompts contain useful diverse comparisons and downweighting reduces performance.
items.risk_reason: The evaluation distribution may legitimately include frequent prompt types.
items.mitigation: Cap rather than eliminate repeats; report row-weighted and group-weighted metrics.
items.rationale: Cheap data/weight audit; likely a small effect and still needs a training run.
items.revision: Distinguished repeated prompts from the tiny set of conflicting repeated comparisons in H12.

items.title: Longer-context training
items.claim: Training and inference with more retained context may improve truncated comparisons.
items.basis: 20.05% of dev inputs truncate. The existing 2,048-token inference pilot gained 0.00464 with interval [-0.00114,0.01072]; that is inconclusive. After H03, unchanged packing gives loss1.013582 on1152 clipped dev rows versus0.939146 on4594 uncut rows; both improve. This slice association is confounded by length/content and does not prove longer context helps.
items.first_test: Expand the fixed inference pilot first, then compare 1,024 versus 2,048 training at matched exposure; try 4,096 only if 2,048 warrants it.
items.acceptance: Overall paired loss gain survives longer-context training and full-test throughput profiling.
items.stop: Stop if gains are confined to a few rows, intervals remain uninformative after the capped pilot, or runtime prevents deployment.
items.risk_reason: Longer inputs reduce training exposure per hour and may exceed inference limits.
items.mitigation: Report changed-input slice and overall loss, equal-token/equal-wall comparisons and actual packed-length timing.
items.rationale: Measured truncation motivates a test, but current evidence does not support treating this as the main cure.
items.revision: Inference-only context results do not estimate a trained long-context model; gain is uncertain and compute-heavy. Updated with final v2 retention slices; keep the causal context comparison and runtime gate.

history.note: Record final H03 clipped/uncut losses1.013582/0.939146 with unchanged packing; confounding prevents a causal longer-context claim. Preserve the bounded matched context test for carryover.

items.title: Adaptive question budget
items.claim: Some question constraints may survive better with adaptive allocation than the fixed 256-token cap.
items.basis: The cap is real in JointTokenizer, but lost-question coverage and recoverable target signal have not been quantified.
items.first_test: Measure which rows and constraints change without labels, then test capped adaptive allocation at the same total context budget. A frozen-model pilot screens for harm; a matched retrain tests the final claim.
items.acceptance: Improve overall loss and the changed-question slice without harming rows whose answers lose budget.
items.stop: Stop if few inputs change or additional question tokens remove more useful answer evidence.
items.risk_reason: More question tokens mean fewer answer tokens at fixed context; inference-only packing creates distribution shift.
items.mitigation: Hold total budget constant, record field retention, and compare packing with matched retraining.
items.rationale: Useful packing ablation, demoted from the original first wave until affected coverage is known.
items.revision: A fixed cap is not evidence of a large recoverable score gap.

items.title: Turn-aligned serialization
items.claim: Preserving chronological request-response alignment may improve multi-turn comparison.
items.basis: Multi-turn cases have higher observed loss, but constitute a minority and are inherently different tasks.
items.first_test: Preserve original turn arrays before flattening, serialize both candidates in aligned chronology, and compare at identical token budgets/exposure.
items.acceptance: Improve overall and multi-turn loss with explicit retention and order-symmetry checks.
items.stop: Stop if gains disappear when retained content is matched or single-turn regressions offset them.
items.risk_reason: An apparent serialization gain may actually be changed truncation; existing flattened caches may have lost turn boundaries.
items.mitigation: Use original parsed turns, test alignment invariants and include content-matched controls.
items.rationale: A sensible representation test, but limited coverage and no direct causal result yet.
items.revision: Demoted from first wave; the aggregate multi-turn association does not prove a layout defect.

items.title: Hierarchical long-text comparison
items.claim: Chunk encoding plus learned aggregation may retain evidence beyond one truncated context.
items.basis: Truncation is measured, but cheap longer-context approaches have not yet shown a reliable gain.
items.first_test: Only after H23, encode chunks with position/turn metadata and compare a small trainable aggregator with equal-budget long-context inference.
items.acceptance: Improve overall loss with acceptable per-row chunk counts and full-test runtime.
items.stop: Stop if chunk independence loses cross-answer relationships or its cost exceeds a larger single pass.
items.risk_reason: Chunking can hide contradictions across boundaries and multiply compute.
items.mitigation: Preserve chunk provenance and cross-answer aggregation; cap chunks and profile realistic long rows.
items.rationale: Complex fallback after simpler context/packing tests.
items.revision: Long-text coverage alone does not justify a new multi-stage architecture.

items.title: Salient extractive retention
items.claim: A label-free extractive policy may preserve decisive middle spans better than head/tail truncation.
items.basis: Some reviewed errors omit middle content; population benefit is unmeasured.
items.first_test: Freeze a deterministic request/claim/code-span selector using training data only and compare retained content plus matched packing/training.
items.acceptance: Improve overall and changed-input loss without excessive preprocessing or shorter-input regressions.
items.stop: Stop if selection systematically omits counterevidence, definitions or caveats.
items.risk_reason: A heuristic can preferentially retain persuasive claims and discard evidence against them.
items.mitigation: Audit retained/dropped spans on a representative train sample and keep both candidate budgets symmetric.
items.rationale: Cheaper and more auditable than generated compression, but still speculative.
items.revision: Retention policies must be label-independent; selected worst cases cannot define the test set.

items.title: Task-aware generated compression
items.claim: A faithful compression stage might improve usable evidence per context token.
items.basis: No compression fidelity or preference benefit has been measured.
items.first_test: After the extractive control, generate train-only summaries without winner labels; independently audit preservation of constraints, facts and competing evidence before a small classifier test.
items.acceptance: Improve human-vote loss beyond extraction, including all compression runtime.
items.stop: Stop on factual hallucination, omitted decisive evidence or an infeasible two-stage submission budget.
items.risk_reason: Summaries can erase exactly the differences being judged, invent facts or introduce teacher preference bias.
items.mitigation: Never expose target labels to compression; retain provenance and original-text fallbacks in the experiment.
items.rationale: High complexity and information-loss risk; cheaper retention comes first.
items.revision: A shorter representation is not necessarily a faithful or sufficient one.

items.title: Human-preference prompt rubric
items.claim: The prompted judge may benefit from a rubric better aligned with voter choices.
items.basis: The blind review did not prove that factuality is overweighted. General judge quality is currently no better than LoRA with confidence.
items.first_test: Predeclare at most two wording changes, score the same fixed pilot without label-bearing examples, and cross-fit calibration separately. Compare both to the original Gemma prompt and the deployed classifier.
items.acceptance: Improve calibrated loss with uncertainty reported; judge-relative gain must also translate to a useful classifier/cascade result.
items.stop: Stop if gains depend on wording selected from inspected error labels or vanish after calibration.
items.risk_reason: Prompt fishing can overfit 512 inspected rows; subjective rubric changes may worsen factual preferences.
items.mitigation: Cap variants, use inner selection and fixed candidate reporting; no leaderboard prompt search.
items.rationale: A cheap information-gathering pilot, with limited expected overall gain.
items.revision: Replaced the unsupported claim that our judge definitely overweights factual correctness.

items.title: Retrieved training demonstrations
items.claim: A few related training-only preference examples may clarify the judge decision boundary.
items.basis: Not tested; prompts can be ambiguous, but demonstrations consume scarce context.
items.first_test: Retrieve a small fixed number from training groups only, exclude near-duplicate evaluation conversations, and compare at a matched total context budget.
items.acceptance: Cross-fitted judge loss improves enough to compete with the classifier while retention/runtime remain viable.
items.stop: Stop if candidate answers lose decisive tokens or gains rely on near-duplicate vote retrieval.
items.risk_reason: Leaky demonstrations can retrieve the answer label; context consumption and class-order bias can dominate.
items.mitigation: Fold-aware retrieval with overlap auditing, balanced labels and separately logged candidate retention.
items.rationale: Potential rubric assistance, but strong leakage and runtime concerns.
items.revision: Similar examples are useful only if they are legitimate fold-local training evidence.

items.title: Bounded critique before verdict
items.claim: A short comparison step may improve judgments over immediate class-token scoring.
items.basis: The deployed Gemma experiment uses immediate restricted labels; richer reasoning is untested and the current full-test runtime is already tight.
items.first_test: Use a fixed small output-token cap on a representative pilot, then request the class with the same probability extraction/calibration protocol.
items.acceptance: Gain remains after runtime and truncation costs; a restricted cascade is acceptable only if separately validated.
items.stop: Stop if output generation breaks throughput limits, produces unsupported rationales or adds no calibrated gain.
items.risk_reason: Generated critiques may amplify mistaken reasoning, anchoring and latency.
items.mitigation: Bound output, log failures, compare with the same judge/model/template and measure actual token throughput.
items.rationale: Worth a bounded pilot, not an assumed benefit of reasoning.
items.revision: A critique can be wrong and may be deployable only on a small subset.

items.title: Independent reference answer
items.claim: Solving a question before seeing candidate answers may reduce anchoring on fluent false claims.
items.basis: No reference-answer benefit has been measured; some tasks are subjective or underdetermined.
items.first_test: On applicable train/pilot tasks, generate a bounded reference from the question alone and judge using it; compare with H31 and direct judgment.
items.acceptance: Improve overall vote loss after accounting for coverage, incorrect references and total inference cost.
items.stop: Stop if references are often wrong, inapplicable or too expensive.
items.risk_reason: An incorrect reference can make both comparisons confidently wrong; objective reference agreement is not the target.
items.mitigation: Audit reference reliability, allow abstention and retain direct-judge controls.
items.rationale: Expensive and target-mismatched without evidence from a simpler critique.
items.revision: Reference generation is an uncertain evidence source, not an oracle.

items.title: Offline factual retrieval
items.claim: Trusted offline evidence may help factual-question comparisons within its coverage.
items.basis: Factual mistakes are visible, but their frequency, retrieval coverage and relation to votes are unmeasured.
items.first_test: Build a small licensed offline reference index unrelated to competition votes; measure evidence relevance and judge improvement on a representative sample.
items.acceptance: Improve overall vote loss including non-factual rows, with a feasible offline corpus and inference budget.
items.stop: Stop if the corpus has weak coverage, retrieves public competition answers or cannot fit Kaggle storage/runtime.
items.risk_reason: Retrieval can leak benchmark text or attach irrelevant/outdated facts, and corpus preparation is costly.
items.mitigation: Audit provenance, exclude vote datasets, record source dates and allow no-evidence fallback.
items.rationale: A large infrastructure project for a narrow uncertain slice.
items.revision: Offline retrieval is possible in principle, but not a general factuality or preference solution.

items.title: Executable code evidence
items.claim: Isolated execution/static evidence may help a subset of coding comparisons.
items.basis: Some code errors are checkable, but arbitrary responses rarely include sufficient trustworthy tests or environments.
items.first_test: Start with static/parse checks and a tiny applicable subset. Execute only in a real isolated environment with no credentials/network and strict resource limits; derive tests from the request, not the preferred answer.
items.acceptance: Improve applicable-slice and overall preference loss after coverage, false failures and runtime are counted.
items.stop: Do not run arbitrary snippets on the host or in an inadequately isolated Kaggle notebook. Stop if safe execution or useful test coverage is unavailable.
items.risk_reason: Untrusted code execution, missing dependencies and generated wrong tests can produce harmful or misleading evidence.
items.mitigation: Require proven isolation, time/memory/output caps and an abstain path; static analysis remains the first-stage scope.
items.rationale: Potentially objective evidence, but expensive engineering and narrow coverage.
items.revision: A timeout or failed dependency is not proof the answer is bad; execution is gated on isolation.

items.title: Symbolic math verification
items.claim: Constrained arithmetic/symbolic checks may help a subset of math comparisons.
items.basis: Some math claims are mechanically checkable; broad extraction and equivalence reliability have not been measured.
items.first_test: Use a constrained parser for explicit expressions and request conditions; audit extraction and check reliability before adding features.
items.acceptance: Improve covered and overall vote loss without turning parser failures into confident negative judgments.
items.stop: Stop if false extractions, hidden assumptions or unsupported proofs dominate useful checks.
items.risk_reason: Symbolic equivalence depends on domains/assumptions, and unrestricted expression evaluation is unsafe.
items.mitigation: Use allowlisted parsing, explicit assumptions, time limits and abstention on unsupported claims.
items.rationale: Smaller scope than code execution, but a low-coverage auxiliary signal.
items.revision: A calculator is reliable only for a correctly extracted, well-specified claim.

items.title: Structural residual correction
items.claim: A small fold-local residual model may add limited structure information beyond the existing classifier.
items.basis: A prior cross-fitted structural blend gained 0.00073 with interval [-0.00054,0.00199]. Structure-only confirmation loss was 1.03059. V6 style control0.945815 nearly matches strength0.945753 versus calibration0.946628 on inspected confirmation; this is a point observation without a fresh structural-model comparison.
items.first_test: Use existing held-out predictions for a fixed low-capacity nested calibration/residual test. A deployed training-data stack requires true OOF inputs; in-sample training predictions are forbidden.
items.acceptance: A repeatable positive paired overall gain beyond the existing blend, with explicit selection cost and feature exclusions.
items.stop: Stop after the predeclared test if the interval remains compatible with no benefit; do not grow a large feature search.
items.risk_reason: Target-derived EDA fields or in-sample base predictions can create artificial stacking gains.
items.mitigation: Allowlist test-computable text descriptors; exclude canonical_label, IDs, model identities and all winner metadata.
items.rationale: Cheap polish with weak measured upside; no GPU retraining is budgeted for this cache-only scope.
items.revision: This extends an already tested small/uncertain blend, not a new likely breakthrough. V7 carryover review raises priority for a cheap fixed-family nested CPU residual test, after source-specific gains failed. No H36 fit is executed in v7.

history.note: Start one fixed symmetric structural tree residual with nested group fitting and matched calibration, probability-only and linear-style controls; CPU2threads/6GiB/7200s.

Fixed nested structural residual loss0.952887 vs calibration0.953959, gain0.001072 CI[0.000085,0.001972]; probability-only tree control comparison CI crosseszero. Predeclared gate fails; no promotion. CPU29.53s/RSS0.463GiB.

items.title: Diverse preference-model ensemble
items.claim: A second preference model may improve the classifier if its errors are genuinely complementary.
items.basis: We have not established that Gemma improves a calibrated blend. Diversity in names or architectures is not sufficient evidence.
items.first_test: First cross-fit one nonnegative blend weight using cached matched-row probabilities; promote only with full fold-safe predictions. Profile sequential loading and total inference cost.
items.acceptance: A frozen ensemble improves overall loss beyond both components after weight selection, under the actual submission budget.
items.stop: Stop if the fitted second weight is zero, complementarity disappears out of fold, or full-test inference exceeds limits.
items.risk_reason: Correlated errors and tuned weights can produce tiny spurious gains; multiple models consume runtime/storage.
items.mitigation: Fit low-capacity weights within folds, keep both single-model controls and count sequential model loading.
items.rationale: A promising follow-up after one genuinely useful alternative model exists.
items.revision: Compute estimate assumes components/predictions already exist; training a missing second model adds its own full budget.

items.title: Domain-specific experts
items.claim: Specialized models with a learned soft gate might help domains only if a global ensemble is insufficient.
items.basis: No reliable specialist advantage or gate benefit has been demonstrated.
items.first_test: Use fold-safe component predictions to test a small soft gate before training any additional specialist.
items.acceptance: Overall loss improves beyond a constant-weight ensemble with stable domain/small-slice behavior and feasible runtime.
items.stop: Stop if a constant blend works equally well or the gate overfits small domains.
items.risk_reason: Multiple training runs, sparse specialist data and routing errors can outweigh benefits.
items.mitigation: Require H37 evidence first, strongly regularize the gate and cap the number of specialists.
items.rationale: Highest complexity with weak local evidence and many cheaper alternatives.
items.revision: Do not infer specialist need merely from heterogeneous question types.

items.title: Budgeted strong-judge cascade
items.claim: A costly judge may help selected rows if a gate can predict its incremental benefit.
items.basis: H37 current-runtime 2048-row nested blend reduces loss by 0.025007 with positive paired evidence; frozen new-group 1486-row gain 0.021022 CI[0.009262,0.032468]. Full sequential 25 k-row projection 49,446 s/13.74 h fails the declared 7 h guard. Complementarity exists against checkpoint 800, while deployability and complementarity against a better H03 classifier remain unproven. Completed H03 now improves full-dev matched loss to0.954069 (gain0.014803); its source is frozen in results/span_002/research_candidate.json. The old ensemble gains cannot be added to this gain: start by rechecking the latest classifier on identical cached judge rows.
items.first_test: Cache-only first: align the 2048 current-runtime judge rows with the latest accepted classifier, retain both component and full-blend controls, and verify that complementarity persists. Predeclare only two entropy-based routes, highest 10% and 20%, with thresholds learned on training groups; compare deterministic random routing at the same fractions. Fit calibration/weights and choose the route within grouped inner folds; evaluate outer groups with paired group intervals. Routing uses classifier outputs available before any judge request, never labels or cached judge disagreement. Freeze a recipe before any further inference. Only a passing cached result justifies an offline bounded runtime profile using E02.
items.acceptance: At least 0.001 overall log-loss reduction versus the matched classifier with positive paired group evidence on a prespecified larger cohort, within an explicit routed fraction and measured offline full-test runtime including setup, switching and calibration. Reconfirm with the latest classifier before deployment.
items.stop: Stop without GPU work if cheap routing does not predict useful incremental judge evidence, complementarity disappears with the latest classifier, or the useful routed fraction violates the runtime budget. An oracle loss-based route is diagnostic only and cannot support adoption.
items.risk_reason: The hard rows for the classifier may be hard for the judge too; using actual per-row losses to route test rows would be an oracle.
items.mitigation: Fit gates on training folds only; test routing without labels and include model switching/loading overhead.
items.rationale: Prioritize the zero-GPU cached pilot: a statistically supported complementary component is already available, but the full ensemble is too slow. Runtime packing E02 is required before a real offline deployment profile, not before this cached test.
items.revision: Reprioritized after measured H37 complementarity and runtime failure. Replace the vague expensive initial gate with two bounded cached entropy routes and matched random controls; model training is not part of this pilot. H37 replaces the unrelated H01 dependency. Do not assume an updated H03 classifier retains checkpoint 800 ensemble gains. Final v2 handoff adds completed H03 as an explicit dependency and latest-model comparator; no new cascade or conditional-blend experiment has been run.

items.title: Constrained probability calibration
items.claim: A low-capacity symmetric extension to temperature scaling may recover a small remaining calibration error.
items.basis: Temperature already improved loss by 0.00856; the extra tie-intercept pilot gained only 0.00170 with interval [-0.00017,0.00332]. Span 001 additionally found paired-model mean tie probability 0.286 versus prevalence 0.315, stable tie AUC, and a class-loss tradeoff that erased order-bias gains.
items.first_test: Predeclare temperature-plus-tie or an A/B-symmetric vector calibration, cross-fit within the cached held-out rows and compare against deployed temperature scaling.
items.acceptance: Positive paired overall gain after nested calibration selection, stable A/B symmetry and normalized probabilities.
items.stop: Stop if gains appear only when fitting and evaluating the same rows, or a richer map is unstable.
items.risk_reason: A flexible calibrator can overfit repeatedly inspected dev examples and reintroduce order bias.
items.mitigation: Keep very few parameters, enforce swap symmetry and publish cross-fitted rather than in-sample metrics.
items.rationale: Very cheap measured-adjacent polish, but not a plausible route to most of the 0.17 gap.
items.revision: Temperature scaling is already deployed; forecast only incremental gain beyond it. Reprioritized as a zero-GPU v2 control after span-001 tie drift; this is planning only and was not executed in v1.

items.title: Recover reward-backbone tie information from pooled pair features
items.claim: The scalar reward bottleneck may discard pairwise tie information that frozen answer representations retain.
items.basis: Span-001 H01 calibrated loss is 1.01557 vs LoRA 0.97635; tie AUC is 0.593 vs 0.660 and tie recall 35.6% vs 44.0%. Forced winner accuracy on 701 human-decisive rows is nearly equal (69.6% vs 69.8%). This is a diagnostic hypothesis, not evidence the richer reward model will beat LoRA. H11 subsequently found that the 69-parameter rich factorized head lost 0.00579 against its probability-only control and did not improve tie AUC on the LoRA backbone.
items.first_test: Reuse the pinned reward checkpoint and fixed sample IDs; extract frozen per-answer hidden representations. Fit the same fold-local symmetric and coupled heads used in H11. Compare against the existing scalar-reward map and the frozen LoRA reference with identical packing/calibration.
items.acceptance: Promote only if richer features improve reward-relative overall loss and provide credible overall benefit or complementarity against LoRA, with paired group intervals and tie/winner decomposition. Report matched head parameter counts.
items.stop: Stop if richer representations leave the reward system materially worse than LoRA, if tie gains merely move a probability intercept, or if renewed data/runtime cost exceeds the declared pilot budget.
items.risk_reason: The reward representation itself may lack human-vote signal; the current scalar system is already worse. Reused inspected development data can overstate a selected feature-head gain.
items.mitigation: Keep this low priority; wait for H11 controls, cap the feature and head search, use training-only PCA/head selection and grouped exploratory evaluation. Preserve the scalar baseline and report unknown pretraining overlap. Do not copy the fixed-PCA recipe unchanged after this negative H11 result; require a better representation/head diagnostic before renewing extraction.
items.rationale: A bounded follow-up distinguishes discarded tie information from generally weak transfer before expensive reward fine-tuning or distillation. The scalar reward system is already 0.039 worse than LoRA, so recovering that gap is a prerequisite for a deployed-baseline gain.
items.revision: New task discovered during v1 from measured H01 tie failures; it is a reward-specific frozen-feature diagnostic, distinct from the LoRA-backed H11 pilot. Planning range corrected to include the measured 0.039 baseline deficit; the range is relative to LoRA, not relative to the scalar reward head. Deprioritized after negative H11 controls; retain as a deferred conditional diagnostic, not a supported promotion path.

history.note: Measured reward utility transfers winner ranking about as well as LoRA but has substantially weaker tie discrimination; test the representation/scalar bottleneck before expensive teacher work.

H11 did not validate the proposed rich fixed-PCA head recipe, while the scalar reward system remains 0.039 worse than LoRA. Retain this v2 diagnostic at P4 and require a better representation/head justification before renewed GPU extraction; no v2 experiment was executed.

items.title: Instrument accepted optimizer updates and training exposure
items.claim: Direct per-cycle logging can make future optimizer and data-exposure comparisons auditable instead of relying only on nominal Trainer steps.
items.basis: Every span-001 arm reached 64 nominal cycles but only 61 accepted updates reconstructed from the pinned scheduler. Processed-token totals include skipped cycles; individual skipped-cycle identities and accepted-token/row exposure were not instrumented.
items.first_test: Record nominal cycle, optimizer-step skip flag, accepted-update counter, GradScaler scale, scheduler position, processed tokens and private sampled-row identities. Verify a tiny forced-overflow probe against actual parameter changes; publish aggregates only. Pin the Trainer/Accelerate versions and include counters in resume state.
items.acceptance: Skipped cycles leave parameters unchanged; accepted counters and scheduler state agree; processed versus accepted exposure and class/group coverage are distinct and reproducible. A short resume preserves these counters.
items.stop: Do not repeat v1 training merely to add retrospective logging. Limit GPU verification to fifteen minutes; withhold long comparisons if the instrumentation cannot identify valid updates.
items.risk_reason: Callback timing or framework wrappers can report stale flags; public row-level logs would expose unnecessary data.
items.mitigation: Use pinned public optimizer/scaler signals, a forced-overflow check and private row artifacts; keep only aggregate counters in Git.
items.rationale: The observed three startup skips are material in a 64-cycle pilot. This is a measurement prerequisite, with no direct score-gain claim.
items.revision: Discovered during v1 from actual AMP skips and the limits of scheduler-based reconstruction.

history.note: Four real pilots had 64 nominal cycles but 61 accepted updates; preserve the measurement gap as a v2 prerequisite rather than repeating v1.

items.title: Preserve tie information during paired-order adaptation
items.claim: Tie-preserving adaptation may retain reduced position bias without the current loss regression, if simple calibration cannot already explain the tradeoff.
items.basis: Paired CE+KL reduced raw second-position advantage from +0.08829 to -0.00293 and order disagreement from 35.45% to 26.17%. Tie AUC stayed near 0.659, but mean tie probability fell from 0.330 to 0.286 against prevalence 0.315; tie loss rose from 1.028 to 1.175 and overall loss worsened by 0.00285.
items.first_test: Run H40 on cached frozen and paired predictions first. Stop if calibration alone explains the deficit. Otherwise predeclare two matched arms: paired CE+0.1 KL versus the same objective plus a Bernoulli tie-probability anchor to symmetric, frozen, uncalibrated teacher predictions on training rows (default anchor weight 1.0, frozen in the next protocol). Use E01 to match actual accepted updates, tokens and row/class exposure. Do not feed a dev-fitted calibrator into training.
items.acceptance: After the same calibration control, obtain at least 0.005 overall loss reduction with positive paired group evidence while retaining low order bias and improved tie loss/discrimination. Report gains against both the paired recipe and deployed LoRA; adoption still needs a larger prespecified comparison.
items.stop: Stop without GPU training if H40 already resolves the tradeoff. Stop if anchoring only preserves teacher errors, only shifts a class intercept, or fails overall loss; cap the pilot at two training variants.
items.risk_reason: The teacher may be wrong, anchoring can suppress learning, and repeatedly inspected development rows can favor a chosen correction. The current paired system is already worse than LoRA.
items.mitigation: Gate on H40, use only training-row teacher outputs without a dev-fitted component, instrument exposure through E01, predeclare one anchor weight and use grouped exploratory evaluation with no claim of untouched generalization.
items.rationale: The observed A/B-versus-tie cancellation motivates a distinct training-objective test; this is not another execution of generic calibration H40 or the original KL-only contrast. Forecasts are relative to deployed LoRA and are not additive with calibration gains.
items.revision: New v2 follow-up from measured v1 order and tie behavior; no execution during v1.

items.title: Blend conditional winner preferences while preserving the tie channel
items.claim: A conditional-winner blend with a fixed classifier tie channel may differ from full-vector blending, but worse human-tie class loss alone does not imply its aggregate tie channel is worse.
